- GILL = https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/daniel-3.html
- PULP = https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/daniel/3.htm
- PULP2 = https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/daniel-3.html

- CON = https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/daniel-3.html (Constable)

---

**Introduction / date**
- Both Greek versions of Daniel date the event to Nebuchadnezzar's 18th year. Ellicott says no one knows where that tradition came from and that Josephus didn't know it. ELL
- If that Greek date is right, the events fall around 587–586 BC, close to Jerusalem's destruction. PA; NET
- Guzik says the timing is debated: soon after Daniel 2, or many years later. EW

**v. 1**
- Guzik sees a link to the dream in Daniel 2. By making the whole statue gold, Nebuchadnezzar was claiming his reign would never end, against God's stated plan. EW
- Guzik thinks it was more like a stylised obelisk (about 90 ft by 9 ft), probably wood covered in gold. EW
- Ellicott also thinks it was wood plated with gold. Because it is so tall for its width, the 60 cubits probably include a pedestal. ELL
- Ellicott suggests it honoured a god (possibly Bel-Merodach) rather than the king himself, partly because of the "sacred numbers" 6 and 60. ELL
- Constable places Dura about six miles south-east of Babylon. The word means "fortification" or "enclosed place." CON
- Gill cites Jewish tradition that Nebuchadnezzar was trying to revive the Babel builders' plan to "make us a name" (Gen 11:4). GILL

**vv. 2–3**
- "Satrap" is a Persian loanword. Requiring every official to attend made the image a test of loyalty. EW
- Constable defines each rank of official. CON
- Ellicott: "sent" means he sent heralds. ELL
- Gill: the officials "stood" ready to bow at the word of command, eager to do whatever the king wanted. GILL
- Bible.org: the king was trying to unite his many peoples under one shared religion. Polytheists could simply add this idol to their gods; Jews could not. BORG

**v. 4**
- "Peoples, nations, languages" means every group in the empire, whatever its language or government. ELL
- The Aramaic word for "herald" may be borrowed from Greek or from Persian; scholars disagree. NET

**v. 5**
- The words for zither, harp and pipes come from Greek. NET
- Critics use these Greek loanwords to argue Daniel was written late. Guzik answers that Greeks were present in the region from the 8th century BC. EW
- Ellicott makes the same case at length, citing Greek–Assyrian contact and Alcaeus's brother serving in Nebuchadnezzar's army. He thinks *sumphonia* may mean a piece of music played together rather than an instrument. ELL
- The Pulpit Commentary notes that Driver held these words "demand" a date in the period of Syrian rule. It calls that a biased judgement. PULP

**v. 6**
- Babylon did use burning as a punishment (Jer 29:22). At a national festival, refusing to worship would count as high treason. ELL
- Guzik also calls the king's view treason. He gives modern examples of rulers using religion to hold on to power. EW

**v. 7**
- Baldwin, quoted by Guzik: literally "as soon as they were hearing they were falling down," so obedience was instant. Guzik also notes music's power for good or evil. EW
- Gill: people bowed out of love of music, fear of the furnace, superstition and the king's order. GILL
- Pulpit: the three may have stood out by staying upright among the bowed crowd. PULP2

**v. 8**
- "Maliciously accused" is literally "ate the pieces of," a vivid idiom for slander. NET; PA
- "Chaldeans" here means native Babylonians, not the astrologer class of Daniel 2. Their motive was jealousy at the Jews' promotion. ELL
- Constable: they were nobles who might gain the three men's posts. CON
- Pulpit: the charge is against "the Jews" as a whole, with the three singled out as test cases. PULP
- The men had not made a show of defying the king; it took informers to expose them. PA; EW

**v. 9**
- "May you live forever" was normal court courtesy and need not be sincere. NET
- Pulpit agrees it is typical Eastern flattery. PULP

**vv. 10–12**
- *Where was Daniel?*
  - Ellicott suggests his rank made attendance unnecessary or that he was away on duty. He adds that a made-up story would also have given Daniel a miracle. ELL
  - Pulpit suggests official duty or illness, and says Daniel's unexplained absence points to the book being old and genuine. PULP
  - NET: Hippolytus guessed Daniel watched from a distance. NET
  - Gill: perhaps he was too high in favour to be touched. GILL
- Their high posts explain both the king's anger (he saw ingratitude) and their enemies' jealousy. ELL
- Constable: the charge was really disloyalty to the king. CON

**vv. 13–14**
- "Is it true?" means literally "Is it on purpose?" ELL
- Constable: the king gave them a second chance, and he distinguished serving his gods from bowing to the image. CON
- "Furious with rage" pairs two words for one idea. NET
- Guzik credits the king for not acting on hearsay. He quotes Spurgeon: holding to your stand when asked "Is it true?" is the harder test. EW

**v. 15**
- The Aramaic sentence breaks off after "if you are ready…"; there is no "good!" in the original. With "what god…?" the king defies every god, his own included. ELL
- Guzik: the king acts more like a secularist whose real god is himself. EW
- The Expositor's Bible calls this an offer of a chance to repent. EXP
- Pulpit hears contempt as well as anger. PULP
- Precept Austin contrasts this question with the king's later confession in v. 29. PA

**v. 16**
- They use his name to match his address to them. Ellicott says the gap between king and subject vanished once the king's order clashed with duty to God. ELL
- "We have no need" is the right sense of the KJV's "we are not careful." ELL
- Constable: "we" is emphatic, implying God would answer for them. CON
- NET suggests repunctuating the line so they say "O king" rather than the over-familiar "O Nebuchadnezzar." NET
- Matthew Henry: they did not need to think about it; the second commandment had already settled the matter. MH

**v. 17** (the BSB's "If the God whom we serve exists" is one way of handling a difficult "if")
- Ellicott: drop the KJV's "so." The sense is "if our God is able… He will deliver." They did not doubt His power, only whether He would choose to use it. He says there is no reason to think they expected a miracle. ELL
- The Expositor's Bible: "able" means "able in accordance with His own plans." EXP
- Guzik takes it as a confident statement of God's power to save them from both the furnace and the king. EW

**v. 18**
- *This is the main place where readers differ, over whether the three expected to be rescued.*
  - Guzik: they did not doubt God's ability, but they did not presume to know His will (compare Job 13:15). He then lists the excuses for compromise they could have made and didn't. EW
  - Gill: if it is not God's will to deliver them, they are content. GILL
  - The Matthew Henry text on Bible Hub: God would deliver them "either from death or in death." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/daniel/3-18.htm
  - The Biblical Illustrator: they were ready for martyrdom but did not seek it. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/daniel/3-18.html
- Guzik: standing firm earlier over the king's food (ch. 1) prepared them for this test. EW
- Matthew Henry makes the same point: faithfulness in small things prepares for greater ones. MH
- The Expositor's Bible calls "And if not" among the most sublime words in Scripture. EXP
- Kay Arthur (on Precept Austin) cites Esther Ahn Kim repeating "but if not." https://www.preceptaustin.org/daniel_-_lecture_5

**v. 19**
- "Seven times" may be a round number, or may allude to Babylon's seven demons. "Than usual" is better rendered "than was fitting." ELL
- Pulpit: it is a round number, and Babylon's seven planetary gods could just as well support the book's authenticity. PULP2

**vv. 20–21**
- The strongest soldiers were picked to stand the heat, which suggests the army was present. ELL
- NET says the clothing words are very uncertain. NET
- Ellicott links them to Herodotus's description of Babylonian dress. ELL
- Showers (via Precept Austin): flammable clothes, killing heat and tight bonds all stress how great the miracle was. PA

**v. 22**
- "Urgent" is the same word as "hasty" in 2:15. The executioners' death contrasts with the rescue of the condemned men. ELL

**v. 23**
- In the Greek Septuagint, the Prayer of Azariah, an addition Protestants class as apocrypha, comes between vv. 23 and 24. It appears in the NRSV Catholic Edition. https://www.gotquestions.org/Prayer-of-Azariah.html
- Pulpit discusses the Song of Azariah as an early addition to the book. PULP; PULP2
- (I couldn't reach any Catholic or Orthodox page on how those churches use it.)

**v. 24**
- The Septuagint says the king's attention was caught by the men singing. EW
- The king was watching through the furnace mouth, which was in its side. ELL
- Calvin: God often forces the ungodly to witness His power against their will. https://biblehub.com/library/calvin/commentary_on_daniel_volume_1/daniel_3_24-25.htm

**v. 25 — who was the fourth figure?**
- Guzik: it was the Son of God; Jesus was with them in the fire. EW
- GotQuestions: most Christians see the pre-incarnate Christ. Others say the Angel of the Lord, which may also mean Christ. https://www.gotquestions.org/who-was-in-the-furnace.html
- Ellicott: the Church Fathers saw Christ, but these are a pagan king's words, and in v. 28 he calls the figure an angel. We can only say it was the "Angel of God's presence." ELL
- Pulpit: don't credit the king with Trinitarian ideas. Christians may hold either Christ or an angel. PULP2
- NET: on a polytheist's lips the phrase means "a divine being." NET
- Applications:
  - Spurgeon: the fire burned only their bonds, and they walked at ease. https://www.spurgeon.org/resource-library/sermons/consolation-in-the-furnace/
  - Gill: the furnace pictures trials that purify believers. GILL
  - The Expositor's Dictionary of Texts: Christ is nearest when the furnace is hottest. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/edt/daniel/3.htm

**v. 26**
- The furnace had a door in its side. ELL
- Kay Arthur: it was open at the top with a door at the front. https://www.preceptaustin.org/daniel_-_lecture_5

**v. 27**
- The officials had seen the proof for themselves. GILL
- The cords burned while the clothes were spared, showing a higher power setting the limits. PULP2
- Guzik reads the whole account as a type of the Great Tribulation: the king pictures the Antichrist, the image the one in Revelation 13, the three men Israel, and the absent Daniel the church. EW
- Kay Arthur also links the image to Revelation 13. https://www.preceptaustin.org/daniel_-_lecture_5

**v. 28**
- "Violated the king's command" is literally "transgressed." ELL
- Pulpit: the king only admits that this God exists and is powerful. He now calls the figure of v. 25 an "angel" (or "messenger"). PULP2
- Guzik lists what the verse shows about God and notes they gave their bodies wholly to Him. EW

**v. 29**
- "Say anything offensive" is literally "speaks negligence." NET
- No other god could deliver like this, not even Bel, who could not save the executioners. GILL
- Bible.org: the decree gave the Jewish community in Babylon freedom of religion. BORG
- The Expositor's Bible doubts that Jews in exile ever faced such a choice; it says the evidence points to tolerance. EXP

**v. 30**
- "Promoted" means they were given back their posts. ELL
- Bible.org: chapters 1 and 3 both end with the friends promoted. BORG
